ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Connect DE, and draw DH $\perp$ AB at H, as shown in the figure:\\
$\because$ CD = 2BD, CE = 2AE,\\
$\therefore \frac{CD}{BD}=\frac{CE}{AE}=2$,\\
$\therefore$ DE $\parallel$ AB,\\
$\therefore \triangle CDE \sim \triangle CBA, \triangle DEF \sim \triangle ABF$,\\
$\therefore \frac{DE}{BA}=\frac{CD}{CB}=\frac{2}{3}$, $\frac{DF}{AF}=\frac{DE}{AB}$,\\
$\therefore \frac{DF}{AF}=\frac{DE}{AB}=\frac{2}{3}$,\\
$\because$ DE $\parallel$ AB,\\
$\therefore S_{\triangle ABE}=S_{\triangle ABD}$,\\
$\therefore S_{\triangle ABE} - S_{\triangle ABF}=S_{\triangle ABD} - S_{\triangle ABF}$,\\
$\therefore S_{\triangle AEF}=S_{\triangle BDF}$,\\
$\therefore S_{\triangle AEF}=\frac{2}{5}S_{\triangle ABD}$,\\
$\because BD = \frac{1}{3}BC = \frac{5}{3}$, and $AB = 6$,\\
$\therefore$ when DH is maximal, the area of $\triangle ABD$ is maximal,\\
$\because$ DH $\leq$ BD,\\
$\therefore$ when DH = BD = $\frac{5}{3}$, the area of $\triangle ABD$ is maximal, and the maximum value is $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{5}{3} \times 6 = 5$,\\
$\therefore$ the maximum area of $\triangle AFE$ is $\frac{2}{5} \times 5 = \boxed{2}$,

raw_record.original_question: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB=6$, $BC=5$, points $D$ and $E$ are on $BC$ and $AC$ respectively, $CD=2BD$, $CE=2AE$, and $BE$ intersects $AD$ at point $F$. What is the maximum area of $\triangle AFE$?
raw_record.answer: Connect $DE$, and draw $DH \perp AB$ at $H$. Since $CD = 2BD$ and $CE = 2AE$, we have $\frac{CD}{BD}=\frac{CE}{AE}=2$, so $DE \parallel AB$. Therefore $\triangle CDE \sim \triangle CBA$ and $\triangle DEF \sim \triangle ABF$. Hence $\frac{DE}{BA}=\frac{CD}{CB}=\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{DF}{AF}=\frac{DE}{AB}=\frac{2}{3}$. Because $DE \parallel AB$, $S_{\triangle ABE}=S_{\triangle ABD}$, so $S_{\triangle AEF}=S_{\triangle BDF}$. Thus $S_{\triangle AEF}=\frac{2}{5}S_{\triangle ABD}$. Since $BD = \frac{1}{3}BC = \frac{5}{3}$ and $AB = 6$, when $DH$ is maximal, the area of $\triangle ABD$ is maximal. Because $DH \leq BD$, when $DH = BD = \frac{5}{3}$, the maximum area of $\triangle ABD$ is $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{5}{3} \times 6 = 5$. Therefore the maximum area of $\triangle AFE$ is $\frac{2}{5} \times 5 = 2$.
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a triangle ABC, where B and C are on the lower same straight-line base BC, and A is above; D is located on BC, E is located on AC; line segment AD and BE intersect at the interior point F. Reasoning: By the coordinate method, let B=(0,0), C=(5,0). Set A=(x,y), since AB=6, so x^2+y^2=36. From CD=2BD and BC=5, obtain BD=5/3, therefore D=(5/3,0). From CE=2AE, obtain AE:EC=1:2, so E is the trisection point on AC from A to C, E=(2A+C)/3=((2x+5)/3,2y/3). Set F on AD, F=A+t(D-A). At the same time F is on BE. Solving the intersection point of the two straight lines gives t=3/5, therefore F=A+(3/5)(D-A)=(1+2x/5,2y/5). Use the determinant to calculate the area of △AFE: S=1/2 |det(F-A,E-A)|. Among them F-A=(1-3x/5,-3y/5), E-A=((5-x)/3,-y/3), the determinant simplifies to 2y/3, so the area is y/3. Because x^2+y^2=36, and in the figure A is above BC, so y≤6, the maximum y=6, obtained when AB is perpendicular to BC. Therefore the maximum area of △AFE is 6/3=2.
